formulas.note: Equal time → ratio of capitals. Equal capital → ratio of times.

formulas.text: Partner's share = (his capital-months ÷ total capital-months) × total profit
Total profit = known share × (sum of ratio parts) ÷ (his ratio part)
formulas.note: For questions that give one partner's share and ask for the total.

formulas.text: Joins after m months (of a 12-month year) → invests for (12 − m) months
formulas.note: 'At the end of 7 months' means he is in for the remaining 5 months.

formulas.text: Capital that changes: add up (capital × months at that capital) for each stretch
formulas.note: A withdrawal after 4 months of ₹20,000 from ₹80,000 → 80,000×4 + 60,000×8.

formulas.text: Working partner's total = commission + his ratio share of the balance, where balance = profit − commission
formulas.note: The commission comes out before the ratio split. Never take his ratio share of the full profit.

formulas.text: If a animals of type A eat as much as b animals of type B, then 1 A = (b/a) B
formulas.note: 3 cows = 7 goats means a cow counts as 7/3 goat (a cow is the bigger eater).

formulas.text: Rent share ∝ (number of animals × months), after converting every animal to one common unit

q-pt-two.standard: Multiply each partner's capital by his months. Write the ratio, add the parts, take his part ÷ total × profit. For 'find total profit', divide the known share by his fraction.
q-pt-two.fast: Cancel common factors before multiplying: 90,000×8 : 1,50,000×5 → 9×8 : 15×5 = 72 : 75 = 24 : 25. Drop zeros and common factors first, then work with the small numbers.
q-pt-two.ultra: Profit ÷ (sum of parts) first, then multiply by his part: 50,000 ÷ 49 ≈ 1,020 → ×25 ≈ 25,510. If the given share divides exactly by his ratio part (18,900 ÷ 7 = 2,700) your ratio is almost certainly right.
q-pt-two.eliminate: (1) Compare the capital-months roughly: 7,20,000 against 7,50,000 are close, so Q gets just over half of 50,000 (about 25,000 to 26,000). Only ₹25,510 is that close; ₹32,000 and ₹35,000 are far too big. (2) When the numbers are nice, a share is a whole multiple of profit ÷ sum of parts: 60,000 ÷ 5 = 12,000, so only ₹24,000 can be P's share.
traps: Ignoring time and splitting by capital alone.
Giving the answer for the wrong partner (read who the question asks for).
In 'find total profit', multiplying by the wrong fraction (use his part, not the other partner's).

q-pt-late.standard: Find each partner's months in the business (12 − months before joining). Multiply capital × months, make the ratio, then share the profit.
q-pt-late.fast: Put the capitals in thousands and divide the capital-months by a common factor: 1,200 : 1,050 : 1,000 → ÷50 → 24 : 21 : 20. Tushar = 20 of 65 parts = 4/13.
q-pt-late.ultra: Reduce the final fraction before multiplying: 20/65 = 4/13, then 1,50,000 ÷ 13 ≈ 11,538 → ×4 = 46,154. Use 1/13 ≈ 0.0769 as a quick check.
q-pt-late.eliminate: (1) Tushar has the smallest capital-months (1,000 against 1,200 and 1,050), so his share is under one third of 1,50,000, which is ₹50,000. That drops ₹55,000. (2) The three are nearly equal, so he gets about 30%, around ₹45,000. That drops ₹35,500. (3) Between ₹46,154 and ₹45,250: the fraction 4/13 does not divide 1,50,000 evenly, so the exact answer is not a round number, which points to ₹46,154.
traps: Counting months before joining instead of months after (joined at month 5 → he stays 7 months, not 5).
Forgetting that the founder stays all 12 months.

q-pt-working.standard: Take the working partner's % off the profit first. Share the balance in the investment ratio. His total = commission + his share of the balance.
q-pt-working.fast: Total fraction = c% + (1 − c%) × his ratio part. For 15% and 2 : 7 → 0.15 + 0.85 × 2/9 = 0.3389. Then × profit.
q-pt-working.ultra: Choose the split that divides cleanly: 81,000 is a multiple of 9, so 2/9 of the balance is easy. 68,850 ÷ 9 = 7,650 → ×2 = 15,300; add 12,150 → 27,450.
q-pt-working.eliminate: Squeeze 2/9 between 1/5 and 1/4. Then M's total is between 15% + 0.85 × 20% = 32% of the profit (₹25,920) and 15% + 0.85 × 25% = 36.25% (₹29,363). Only ₹27,450 fits; ₹24,000, ₹30,000 and ₹33,000 are all outside.
traps: Taking his ratio share of the full profit and then adding the commission (double counting).
Taking the commission as a % of his own share instead of the whole profit.
Forgetting to add the commission to his total.

q-pt-pasture.standard: Pick one animal as the standard. Convert every other animal using the given equivalence. Multiply animals × months for each person, then split the rent in that ratio.
q-pt-pasture.fast: Pick the unit so that every equivalent becomes a whole number. 2 oxen = 5 goats and 3 goats = 4 sheep → in 'thirds of a sheep': ox = 10, goat = 4, sheep = 3. Then no fractions appear anywhere.
q-pt-pasture.ultra: After converting, cancel the common factor of the two totals: 1,140 : 1,212 → ÷12 → 95 : 101. Fraction = 95/196. Check the direction first: 3 cows = 7 goats means 1 cow = 7/3 goat, not the other way round.
q-pt-pasture.eliminate: Estimate the fraction: X's total ≈ 285, Y's ≈ 303, so X ≈ 285/588 ≈ 0.485, a little under half. Any option above ½ or far below it is out. This leaves 90/196 (0.459) and 95/196 (0.485), and one rough division settles it.
traps: Reading the equivalence upside down (cow worth 3/7 goat instead of 7/3).
Leaving one animal type out of a person's total.

pyqs.text: P puts in ₹90,000 for 8 months and Q puts in ₹1,50,000 for 5 months. Profit is ₹50,000. Find Q's share (approximate).
pyqs.trick: Compare 7,20,000 with 7,50,000 first: nearly equal, so the answer is just over half of ₹50,000.

a.note: Q's capital-months (7,50,000) are larger than P's (7,20,000), so Q gets more than half of ₹50,000. ₹20,000 is below half.

b.note: The two capital-months are within 4% of each other (24 : 25), so Q's share is only just over half. ₹32,000 would be 64%.

c.note: Same reason: ₹35,000 would be 70% of the profit, far from a 24 : 25 split.

pyqs.text: P and Q invest ₹50,000 and ₹75,000 for the same period. Find P's share of a ₹60,000 profit.
solution: Time is equal, so the ratio is the capital ratio 50 : 75 = 2 : 3.
pyqs.trick: 2 : 3 means 5 equal parts of ₹12,000. P's share must be a multiple of ₹12,000, and only ₹24,000 is.

a.note: 2 : 3 makes 5 parts of ₹12,000 each, so P's share is a multiple of ₹12,000. ₹18,000 is not.

b.note: 2 : 3 makes 5 parts of ₹12,000 each, so P's share is a multiple of ₹12,000. ₹22,000 is not.

d.note: 2 : 3 makes 5 parts of ₹12,000 each, so P's share is a multiple of ₹12,000. ₹26,000 is not.

pyqs.text: C invests ₹1,40,000 for 9 months and D invests ₹1,80,000 for 8 months. C's share of profit is ₹18,900. Find the total profit.
pyqs.trick: C has 7 of 15 parts, so 18,900 ÷ 7 = 2,700 a part. The total is 15 × 2,700.

b.note: With a total of ₹36,000, C (7 of 15 parts) would get ₹16,800, not ₹18,900.

c.note: With a total of ₹34,200, C (7 of 15 parts) would get ₹15,960, not ₹18,900.

d.note: With a total of ₹38,400, C (7 of 15 parts) would get ₹17,920, not ₹18,900.

pyqs.text: Rajesh starts with ₹1,00,000. Suresh joins after 5 months with ₹1,50,000. Tushar joins at the end of 7 months with ₹2,00,000. Yearly profit ₹1,50,000. Find Tushar's share (approximate).
solution: Months in business: Rajesh 12, Suresh 12 − 5 = 7, Tushar 12 − 7 = 5.
pyqs.trick: Three nearly equal capital-months with Tushar the smallest: expect just under a third of ₹1,50,000.

a.note: Tushar has the smallest capital-months (1,000 against 1,200 and 1,050), so he gets less than a third of ₹1,50,000, i.e. under ₹50,000.

c.note: A near miss: ₹45,250 is 30.2% of the profit, but Tushar's fraction is 20/65 = 30.8%.

d.note: Tushar holds about 31% of the capital-months (1,000 of 3,250), so he gets over ₹45,000. ₹35,500 is only 24%.

pyqs.text: M and N invest in the ratio 2 : 7 and earn ₹81,000. M works in the business and gets 15% of the profit extra. Find M's total share.
pyqs.trick: Squeeze 2/9 between 1/5 and 1/4: M gets 15% + 0.85 × (20% to 25%) = 32% to 36% of ₹81,000.

a.note: M's total is at least 15% + 0.85 × 20% = 32% of the profit = ₹25,920. ₹24,000 is below that.

c.note: M's total is at most 15% + 0.85 × 25% = 36.25% of the profit = ₹29,363. ₹30,000 is above that.

d.note: Above the same ceiling of ₹29,363; ₹33,000 would be 41% of the profit.

pyqs.text: X keeps 18 oxen for 5 months and 20 goats for 3 months. Y keeps 24 goats for 7 months and 30 sheep for 6 months. 2 oxen eat as much as 5 goats, and 3 goats as much as 4 sheep. What fraction of the rent does X pay?
solution: Use units of one-third sheep: sheep = 3, goat = 4 (3 goats = 4 sheep), ox = 10 (1 ox = 2.5 goats).
pyqs.trick: After converting, 1,140 : 1,212 is nearly 1 : 1, so X pays just under half. Cancel ÷12 to get 95 : 101.

a.note: A rough count puts X at 1,140 and Y at 1,212 units, so X pays about 48.5%. 90/196 is 45.9%.

c.note: Both keep many animals for many months, so X pays close to half, not 5%.

d.note: X's total (1,140) is smaller than Y's (1,212), so X pays less than half. 111/196 is above half.

pyqs.text: M keeps 12 cows for 4 months and 18 goats for 5 months. N keeps 26 goats for 7 months. 3 cows are equivalent to 7 goats. Find M's share of the rent.
solution: Use units of one-third goat: goat = 3, cow = 7 (1 cow = 7/3 goat).
pyqs.trick: Cow ≈ 2.3 goats, so M ≈ 112 + 90 = 202 against N = 182: M pays about 52.6%.

b.note: Estimate: a cow is about 2.3 goats, so M ≈ 202 and N = 182 goat-months, i.e. M ≈ 52.6%. 110/192 is 57%.

d.note: M keeps more animals for more months than N's share would allow at 31%.
